Read About Belgrade

A city rebuilt more than forty times, where a Habsburg river town and an Ottoman hill fortress still argue across the water.

A city that keeps getting knocked down

Belgrade sits on the invasion route between two empires, and it shows. The Celts had a hilltop settlement here before the Romans built a legionary fortress on the same bluff; the Byzantines, the medieval Serbian kings, the Ottomans and the Habsburgs each took a turn holding the confluence of the Sava and the Danube, and each left something behind before losing it again. Historians count somewhere north of forty sieges and destructions across the city's recorded history — a number Belgraders repeat with a kind of dark pride rather than complaint. Kalemegdan, the fortress park that opens this guide's first day, is the clearest single place to see the layering: Roman well shafts, an Ottoman gunpowder magazine, and a Cold War bunker sit within a few hundred metres of each other, none of them fully replacing what came before.

The fortress the city grew from is also the fortress the city keeps rebuilding around.

Two cities in one, on either side of a park

What surprises first-time visitors is how legible the empires still are on the ground. Skadarlija, the cobbled bohemian quarter behind Republic Square, was settled by Roma musicians and gypsy blacksmiths in the 1830s and later became the address of choice for Serbia's poets and painters — its kafanas still run on the same format of grilled meat, live tamburitza music and rakija that made the street famous a century ago. Walk the other direction, north across the Sava into Zemun, and the register changes completely: pastel Austro-Hungarian townhouses, a Habsburg-era grid of streets, and a hilltop memorial tower built to mark a thousand years of Hungarian settlement on the plain. Zemun was a separate Habsburg border town until 1934, and it still feels like one — a quieter, lower-rise counterpoint to the Ottoman-and-Yugoslav core across the water.

The Yugoslav layer is the most recent, and the rawest

No stretch of Belgrade's history is closer to the surface than the Yugoslav one. Josip Broz Tito is buried in a glass-walled mausoleum on the Dedinje hillside, inside what is now Serbia's most-visited museum — a building that still gets flowers left at the tomb by visitors old enough to remember the country he held together. The Museum of Yugoslavia's other galleries are a room-by-room record of what that country looked like in the gifts foreign leaders sent Tito over three decades: ceremonial swords, hand-woven carpets, a baton passed hand to hand across the whole federation on his birthday. It is not a nostalgic museum, and it does not try to resolve how Yugoslavia is remembered — it simply shows the evidence and lets the visitor do the work.

A river culture that never really stopped

Belgrade's relationship with its two rivers is not scenery — it is where the city actually goes to socialize. A splav is a barge, usually a converted fishing boat, moored along the Sava or Danube bank and run as a bar, restaurant or club; there are dozens of them, and Belgraders choose one the way visitors elsewhere might choose a neighbourhood bar, by its music policy rather than its address. Upstream from the splavovi, Zemunski Kej — the promenade below Gardoš hill — does the same thing at a slower pace: fishing rods propped against the railing, café tables facing the water, families walking the same stretch of riverbank their grandparents walked when Zemun was still its own town across the border. Further out, Great War Island sits at the exact point where the Sava meets the Danube, an uninhabited nature reserve reachable only by a short boat crossing — proof that even the city's wildest ground is still organized around the water that keeps rebuilding, and re-dividing, Belgrade.
